title: Clarinet influences: Shaw, Goodman, Hall, Bigard
summary: Nicholas on clarinettists he admired and Bigard taking his place.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Who were the great clarinetists? Favorites and rivals

blocks.x: To get back to the early days, did you watch the other clarinet players carefully? Did you watch them to figure out anything?

Yes, you sure you got ears. I tell you, when I was coming up, I admired Artie Shaw was my favorite clarinet player. Benny Goodman, he played nice, but he was a mechanical to me. I didn't copy him, but I knew what they were making. But Artie Shaw had something else. He had a beautiful sound. He was a great musician. And this man was something else. I liked his band, Artie Shaw, in the third. You had another one you had. You had a lot of clarinet players. But it was all imitating Benny. And that was a little, Benny had got a strong tone and was a good musician. I'm not putting that now. But it isn't for me to imitate. It's mechanical. It's something. Now, I like Edmund Hall. He's got soul. Benny ain't got no soul. He play technical, he runs over, beautiful. But Hall had something, he had guts. And who else? Pee Wee Russell. He had guts. He had something else. A little something different, you know, in the clarinet. Oh, he had many of them. Jimmy D'Arcy, he was a good tune. Jimmy D'Arcy. He had his stuff going also. Who else had? Uh, Bonnie B. Dodd came when he went with Duke. Bonnie had something. Bonnie was playing some beautiful clarinet with Duke. Did he play clarinet down here in New Orleans? No. He didn't. He, when I left to go to China in 1924, 1926 rather. Bonnie took my place and he improved on these. And when he went with Duke, I was surprised when I came back, you know, two or three years away.
